title: Head injury: GCS and when to scan

header.contentArea: Applied surgical science and critical care

related.why: The lucid interval and the CT

brief.scenario: Mrs Lowe, 72, fell down a flight of 8 stairs 3 hours ago. She lost consciousness briefly. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. She has vomited once. She opens her eyes spontaneously, is confused, and obeys commands.
brief.task: The examiner will ask about her GCS and whether and when she needs imaging.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Score the GCS by component, then match her to the NICE CT criteria and timings.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Choosing the 8-hour rule when a 1-hour criterion applies.

grid.label: Primary survey
grid.fail: Focuses on the head and ignores airway and cervical spine.
grid.pass: ABCDE with cervical spine protection; glucose; pupils; time of last apixaban dose.
grid.high: Looks for other injuries, such as a hip fracture; suspected neck injury with age 65+ or a fall over 5 stairs: CT cervical spine within 1 hour.

grid.label: GCS technique
grid.fail: Gives only a total, or can't list the components.
grid.borderline: Scores correctly but reports only the total.
grid.pass: Eye 4, verbal 5, motor 6; scores each component, using the best motor response.
grid.high: Reports components with the total every time: E4 V4 M6, GCS 14.

grid.label: CT within 1 hour
grid.pass: GCS 12 or less initially; under 15 at 2 hours; open, depressed or basal skull fracture signs; seizure; focal deficit; more than 1 vomit.
grid.high: Spots that GCS 14 at 3 hours triggers a CT within 1 hour here, ahead of her age or apixaban.

grid.label: CT within 8 hours and anticoagulants
grid.fail: Would observe without a scan because her GCS is 'nearly normal'.
grid.pass: Loss of consciousness or amnesia plus age 65+, a clotting disorder, dangerous mechanism or over 30 minutes' retrograde amnesia: CT within 8 hours.
grid.high: Anticoagulated with no other indication: consider CT within 8 hours. Knows she already qualifies on stronger criteria.

grid.label: Observations and deterioration
grid.pass: Half-hourly GCS until 15; then half-hourly for 2 hours, hourly for 4 hours, 2-hourly after.
grid.high: Names reassessment triggers: sustained 1-point GCS drop, motor drop of 2, new pupil asymmetry, worsening headache or vomiting.

grid.label: Neurosurgery and reversal
grid.fail: Doesn't know when to involve neurosurgery.
grid.pass: Discuss with neurosurgery: GCS 8 or less, confusion over 4 hours, deterioration, progressive focal signs, CSF leak, penetrating injury.
grid.high: For a bleed on apixaban: reversal per NICE and local protocol with haematology; intubate GCS 8 or less for transfer.

grid.label: Handover and explanation
grid.fail: Doesn't explain or document the plan.
grid.pass: SBAR referral with GCS components, mechanism, anticoagulant and injury time.
grid.high: Explains to her family why she needs a scan now and what observations will follow.

fail.text: I'd examine her head for injuries.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: She's nearly normal, so I'd observe her on the ward.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Neuro obs as per the ward.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: We're keeping an eye on her.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: ABCDE with cervical spine protection, glucose and pupils. I'd find out when she last took apixaban.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Eyes open spontaneously 4, confused 4, obeys commands 6: E4 V4 M6, 14.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes. Her GCS is under 15 more than 2 hours after the injury, so CT within 1 hour. Other 1-hour criteria are GCS 12 or less initially, skull fracture signs, seizure, focal deficit, or more than 1 vomit.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: She'd also meet the 8-hour criteria: loss of consciousness, age over 65 and a dangerous fall.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Half-hourly GCS until 15, then half-hourly for 2 hours, hourly for 4, then 2-hourly.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: GCS 8 or less, confusion over 4 hours, deterioration, progressive focal signs, CSF leak or a penetrating injury.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd refer with an SBAR giving the GCS components, the fall, the apixaban and the time.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: ABCDE with cervical spine protection. She's over 65 with a fall down more than 5 stairs, and her neck is tender, so she needs a CT cervical spine within the hour too. Glucose, pupils, her hips, and when she last took apixaban.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: E4 V4 M6, total 14. I'd always give the components with the total.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Yes, within 1 hour: she's 3 hours from the injury and still GCS 14. That criterion comes first; her age and the apixaban would only give her 8 hours.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Even without that, loss of consciousness with age over 65 or a dangerous mechanism means CT within 8 hours, and apixaban alone would make me consider one.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Half-hourly until 15, then half-hourly for 2 hours, hourly for 4, then 2-hourly. I'd reassess urgently for a sustained 1-point drop, a 2-point motor drop, new pupil asymmetry, or worsening headache or vomiting.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any significant bleed on the scan, or deterioration, confusion over 4 hours, progressive focal signs or a CSF leak. With a bleed on apixaban, reversal per NICE and local protocol with haematology.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Her scan is being done now because she's still a little confused 3 hours after the fall and takes a blood thinner. We'll check her closely afterwards and tell you as soon as we have the result.

failures.move: Applying the 8-hour rule when she meets a 1-hour criterion.
failures.consequence: Delays finding a bleed in an anticoagulated patient.

failures.move: Reporting a total GCS without components.
failures.consequence: Hides a falling motor score, the most important sign.
Safety-critical: moving an unprotected neck after a fall down stairs risks cord injury.

recovery.line: Let me break that down: E4 V4 M6, 14.
Actually she's GCS 14 at 3 hours, so she needs a CT within 1 hour.

knowledge.fact: CT within 1 hour: GCS 12 or less initially; under 15 at 2 hours; suspected open, depressed or basal skull fracture; seizure; focal deficit; more than 1 vomit.
CT within 8 hours: loss of consciousness or amnesia plus age 65+, bleeding disorder, dangerous mechanism, or over 30 minutes' retrograde amnesia.
Anticoagulated with no other indication: consider CT within 8 hours of the injury.
Always give GCS components with the total.

recall.think: Components, then the clock: 1 hour or 8 hours?
recall.say: "E4 V4 M6, 14, three hours after injury: CT within the hour."

numbers.meaning: CT if GCS < 15 at 2 h, ≤ 12 initially, and more
CT if LOC/amnesia + age 65+ or other risk

recall.trap: Anticoagulant = 8 hours, even when a 1-hour criterion applies.

partner.opening: This is Mrs Lowe, who fell down the stairs. How would you assess her?

reveals.finding: Talking; collar in place; midline neck tenderness when asked.
Eyes open spontaneously; confused conversation; obeys commands.
Pupils equal and reactive; no focal weakness.
Scalp laceration; no haemotympanum, CSF leak, periorbital or mastoid bruising.

reveals.trigger: Asks when apixaban was last taken

reveals.finding: Small acute subdural haematoma, 4 mm, no midline shift.

push.question: How soon does she need a CT, and why?
push.expect: Within 1 hour: GCS under 15 at 2 hours after the injury.

push.question: What are the reassessment triggers on observations?
push.expect: Sustained 1-point drop, 2-point motor or 3-point eye/verbal drop, pupils, headache, vomiting, agitation.

curveballs.prompt: An hour later she's E3 V3 M5.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Deterioration: urgent reassessment, repeat CT and discuss with neurosurgery now.

curveballs.prompt: She had the fall yesterday and has only just come in.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Presenting over 8 hours after injury with a risk factor: CT within the hour.

curveballs.prompt: Her GCS is 15, no loss of consciousness, no other risk factors, but she takes apixaban.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider a CT within 8 hours of the injury.
